title: From React to Next.js
summary: See what Next.js adds to React, create a Next.js 16 project, and follow one request from the URL to server HTML and a hydrated page.
intro: In the React course, getting real HTML out of a server took a Node server of your own, hydration code, and cache headers, and Server Components were out of reach. Next.js packages all of that. This lesson shows what it adds to React and why there are two routers, then creates the Trailhead project with `create-next-app`, walks through every file it makes, runs it in development and as a production build, and follows one request from the address bar to a page you can click.

steps.title: What React leaves to a framework
steps.body:
Knowing what a framework does for you tells you which problems are now yours and which are its. That matters the first time something goes wrong: you need to know which side to look on.

## What React leaves open

React, as the React course put it, is a library for drawing UI from state, and it leaves three big questions to you: which component shows for which URL, where the data comes from, and where the HTML is made. In a Vite app, the answers were React Router in the browser, TanStack Query in the browser, and an empty `div` that JavaScript fills in, which is client-side rendering, CSR.

The React course's lesson on rendering on the server answered the third question by hand. You rendered with `renderToPipeableStream`, hydrated with `hydrateRoot`, prerendered pages with `prerender`, and set `s-maxage` and `stale-while-revalidate` so a CDN, a network of servers that keep copies of your pages near your visitors, could regenerate them. Each piece worked, and each one was code you had to keep working.

## What Next.js adds

Next.js answers all three questions with conventions, rules about where files go and what they're called. Follow them, and the framework wires the pieces together:

- **Routing from files.** A folder in `app/` is a piece of the URL, and a `page.tsx` inside it is the page. Layouts, loading states, and error pages are files too.
- **Rendering modes.** Each page can be made at build time (static), on every request (dynamic), or as a static shell with fresh parts streamed in, and you choose by how you write it, not with server code.
- **Caching.** You can mark data or a whole component to be kept and reused, and say when it goes stale.
- **Server code in the same project.** Server Components, Server Actions for forms, and Route Handlers for API endpoints live next to your pages.
- **Turbopack**, the bundler, which plays the part Vite played in the React course.
- **Images, fonts, and metadata**, the tags in a page's `head` that search engines and link previews read, handled for you.

## Two routers: Pages and App

Next.js has had two ways to define routes, and you'll meet both at work. The **Pages Router**, from 2016, uses a `pages/` folder. Each file is a page, and a page loads its data with special functions like `getServerSideProps`. Every component in it is a client component that also renders on the server.

The **App Router**, from 2023, uses an `app/` folder, and it's built on React Server Components, so most components never ship to the browser. It's what new projects use, and it's what this course teaches. The Pages Router still works and still gets fixes, so plenty of older projects run on it. The examples below show the same page both ways, so you can tell which one a project uses at a glance.

## It runs where Node.js runs

`next build` turns your project into a production build, and `next start` serves it with an ordinary Node.js server. So a Next.js app runs on your laptop, on a server you rent, in a Docker container, or on a hosting platform. Vercel, the company that makes Next.js, runs one such platform, and others like Netlify and Cloudflare support it too. A site with no server code at all can even be exported as plain files. The Shipping lessons come back to all of these.

examples.title: A page in the Pages Router
examples.prompt: An older project's `pages/products/[slug].tsx`. You'll recognize the Pages Router by its `pages/` folder and functions like `getServerSideProps`.
examples.explanation: Next.js calls `getServerSideProps` on the server for every request, and passes what it returns to the component as props. The component itself is a client component: it renders on the server first, and then all of its code is sent to the browser and hydrated, even though it only shows a heading. Data loading and the UI live in two separate functions, and the data has to travel from one to the other as props. The App Router removes that split.

examples.title: The same page in the App Router
examples.prompt: The App Router version, at `app/products/[slug]/page.tsx`. The page is a Server Component, so it loads its own data.
examples.explanation: One async component does both jobs. It reads the `slug` from the URL through `params`, fetches the product, and returns the heading. `notFound()` shows the 404 page. `PageProps<"/products/[slug]">` is a type Next.js generates from your folders, so `params` is typed for this exact route. The routing lesson covers `params` and `notFound()` in full, and the data lessons show where a fetch like this belongs and how to cache it. Because nothing here runs in the browser, the browser gets the heading as HTML and none of this code.

steps.title: Creating a project
steps.body:
A new project should start from the same setup most teams use, so that what you read in the docs matches what's on your screen. `create-next-app` is the official tool for that. It asks a few questions, writes the starting files, and installs everything.

## Check your Node.js version

Next.js 16 needs Node.js 20.9 or newer. Check yours with `node --version` in a terminal. If it prints `v18` or older, install a newer version from nodejs.org first.

## Create the project

The shop lives in the Playground, like the React course's did. If you kept the React course's shop, it's already there in a folder named `trailhead`, so rename that one first, for example to `trailhead-react`, in the Explorer or with `mv trailhead trailhead-react`. Then, in the Playground's terminal, in the Playground folder, run:

```bash
npx create-next-app@latest trailhead
```

`npx` downloads and runs a package without installing it for good, as you saw in the React course. `@latest` asks for the newest version, and `trailhead` is the name of the folder it will create. It first asks whether you want the recommended defaults:

```text
? Would you like to use the recommended Next.js defaults? › - Use arrow-keys. Return to submit.
❯   Yes, use recommended defaults
    TypeScript, ESLint, No React Compiler, Tailwind CSS, No src/ directory, App Router, Cache Components, AGENTS.md, Agent feedback
    No, reuse previous settings
    No, customize settings
```

Press Enter for **Yes**. Here's what each default means:

- **TypeScript**, the same typed JavaScript you used in the React course.
- **ESLint**, the linter, with rules for React and Next.js.
- **No React Compiler.** The compiler you met in the React course is off by default here. You can turn it on later.
- **Tailwind CSS**, already wired up, the same utility classes you used before.
- **No src/ directory.** The `app/` folder sits at the top of the project instead of inside `src/`.
- **App Router**, the router this course teaches.
- **Cache Components**, the newer caching model, which the data lessons are built on.
- **AGENTS.md**, a note for AI coding tools, which the next part explains.
- **Agent feedback**, an opt-in that lets AI coding tools prepare anonymous feedback about Next.js for you to review before anything is sent.

It also sets up an **import alias**, a short name for a folder: `@/` means the project's root, so `@/lib/products` works from any file, however deep.

If you'd rather skip the question, `npx create-next-app@latest trailhead --yes` takes the defaults straight away.

## What gets installed

`create-next-app` lists the packages as it installs them:

```text
Installing dependencies:
- next
- react
- react-dom

Installing devDependencies:
- @tailwindcss/turbopack
- @types/node
- @types/react
- @types/react-dom
- eslint
- eslint-config-next
- tailwindcss
- typescript
```

The **dependencies** are what the app needs to run: Next.js and React. The **devDependencies** are only needed while you build: TypeScript and its type packages, ESLint with the Next.js rules, and Tailwind with `@tailwindcss/turbopack`, the piece that lets Turbopack run Tailwind on your CSS. While it installs, npm may warn that ESLint 9 is no longer supported. That's ESLint announcing its newer version. The Next.js rules work with the one installed, so you can ignore it.

At the end it creates a git repository with a first commit and prints **Success!**. Then move into the folder with `cd trailhead`.

examples.title: The package.json it writes
examples.prompt: `trailhead/package.json`, as `create-next-app` 16.4.6 wrote it. Your version numbers may be a little newer.
examples.explanation: The four scripts are the commands you'll run most: `npm run dev` while you build, `npm run build` and `npm run start` for a production build, and `npm run lint` to check the code. `next`, `react`, and `react-dom` are pinned to exact versions with no `^`, so everyone on a team gets the same ones. The `^` on the type packages lets npm pick newer minor versions. `private: true` stops anyone from publishing the project to npm by accident. Next.js 16.4 comes with React 19.3, the React version the React course used.

steps.title: The files and folders
steps.body:
You'll open these files every day, and a few of them are generated and must never be edited by hand. Knowing which is which saves you from changes that disappear, and from committing things that don't belong in git.

```diagram react-to-nextjs-tree
The app folder holds your routes. Everything else configures the project, and two folders are generated.
```

## The app folder

`app/` is where the routes live. Every folder inside it is a piece of the URL, and only a folder with a `page.tsx` is a page someone can visit. The fresh project has one route, the home page:

- `app/layout.tsx` is the **root layout**, the component that wraps every page. It's the only place the `html` and `body` tags are written, and it sets the page's title and description through an object called `metadata`.
- `app/page.tsx` is the page at `/`. Edit it, and the home page changes.
- `app/globals.css` imports Tailwind and sets a few colors as CSS variables, with a dark version under `prefers-color-scheme`. It also sets `font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif` on `body`, which hides the Geist font the layout loads everywhere except where a `font-sans` class asks for it. Delete that line to use Geist on the whole site.
- `app/favicon.ico` is the icon in the browser tab. Next.js finds it by its name and adds the right `link` tag for you, one of several files it recognizes by name.

## Files served as is

`public/` holds files the server sends exactly as they are, at the site's root: `public/next.svg` is at `/next.svg`. Use it for images, fonts, and files like `robots.txt` that must sit at a fixed address.

## Configuration

- `next.config.ts` holds Next.js settings. The fresh one turns on `cacheComponents` and `partialPrefetching`, which the routing and data lessons explain, and tells Turbopack to run Tailwind on every CSS file.
- `tsconfig.json` is TypeScript's settings, including the `@/*` alias and a plugin that checks Next.js rules in your editor.
- `eslint.config.mjs` loads the Next.js lint rules: React's rules of hooks, checks for common performance mistakes, and the TypeScript rules.
- `next-env.d.ts` points TypeScript at types Next.js generates, like `PageProps`. Next.js rewrites it on every run, so never edit it.
- `AGENTS.md` tells AI coding tools to read the docs bundled in `node_modules/next/dist/docs` before writing code, since Next.js changes faster than their training. It's good advice for people too.

## Generated folders, and what git ignores

`.next/` is created the first time you run the app. It holds production builds, the dev server's cache, and generated types. `node_modules/` holds the installed packages. Neither belongs in git: anyone can recreate both with `npm install` and `npm run build`. The project's `.gitignore` already lists them, along with `out/` (a static export), `build/`, `next-env.d.ts`, `*.tsbuildinfo` (TypeScript's cache), and `.vercel`.

## Environment variables at a glance

Next.js reads `.env` files on its own, the way Vite did in the React course. A line like `API_URL=http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1` in a `.env` file makes `process.env.API_URL` available to your server code. The big difference from Vite is the prefix: a variable is **server-only** unless its name starts with `NEXT_PUBLIC_`. A `NEXT_PUBLIC_` value is copied into the browser's JavaScript when you build, so anyone can read it, just like a `VITE_` value. Everything else stays on the server.

The `.gitignore` ignores every file that starts with `.env`, so secrets in them never reach git by accident. A line that starts with `!` makes an exception: the security lesson later in the course adds `!.env` and `!.env.example`, so that settings which aren't secret, and a list of the variables the app needs, can be committed, while secrets stay in `.env.local`. It covers environment variables in depth.

examples.title: The root layout
examples.prompt: `app/layout.tsx` as `create-next-app` wrote it. Every page in the app renders inside it.
examples.explanation: `children` is whatever page the URL matched, so this component wraps every page in the same `html` and `body`. `LayoutProps<"/">` is a generated type that knows which props a layout at `/` receives. The `metadata` object becomes the `title` tag and a `meta` description tag in every page's `head`, and the Shipping lessons show how a page overrides it. `Geist` and `Geist_Mono` come from `next/font`, which downloads the fonts when you build and serves them from your own site, so visitors never wait on Google's servers. Their `variable` options turn each font into a CSS variable, which `globals.css` hands to Tailwind. Importing `globals.css` in the root layout applies it to every page. You could import global CSS in other files too, but Next.js doesn't unload a stylesheet when you leave a page, so keep truly global styles here.

examples.title: The Next.js settings
examples.prompt: `next.config.ts` as generated. It's TypeScript, so your editor checks each option's name.
examples.explanation: `cacheComponents: true` turns on Cache Components, the caching model this course teaches: Next.js prerenders every page it can and makes you say clearly which parts must wait for a request. `partialPrefetching: true` makes links download a small shell of the next page ahead of time. Both are new in Next.js 16, and the docs say they'll be on for every app in the next major version. The `turbopack.rules` block runs Tailwind on every `.css` file as Turbopack bundles it. Depending on how you answered the questions, your file may also hold an `experimental` block for agent feedback. A change here takes effect when you restart the dev server.

steps.title: Dev, build, and start
steps.body:
You'll spend most of your time in the dev server, but your users only ever see a production build, and the two behave differently. Knowing what each command does tells you which one to trust when something works in one and not the other.

## Give the shop its own port

Recall from the web course that only one program can listen on a port, and that Hack University itself uses port 3000 on your computer. Next.js starts on port 3000 by default, and it listens on every address the computer has, your Wi-Fi one included, as the Network line it prints shows. So before the first run, open `package.json` and give the `dev` and `start` scripts two options each:

```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "dev": "next dev --hostname 127.0.0.1 --port 3005",
    "build": "next build",
    "start": "next start --hostname 127.0.0.1 --port 3005",
    "lint": "eslint"
  }
}
```

`--port 3005` moves the shop off Hack University's port, and `--hostname 127.0.0.1` keeps it on loopback, so only your own computer can reach it. The rest of the course uses `http://127.0.0.1:3005`. On another project, plain `next dev` on port 3000 is the usual choice, and if that port is taken, `next dev` picks the next free one and warns you.

## next dev

`npm run dev` starts the **dev server**. It compiles each route with Turbopack the first time you open it, so the first visit to a page takes a moment and later ones are quick. It also runs **Fast Refresh**: save a file, and the open page updates in place within a second, keeping the state of client components, like text typed into a field.

The terminal running the dev server is now the **server's** console. A `console.log` in a Server Component prints there, not only in the browser, because that's where the component ran. In development, Next.js also copies those logs into the browser's console with a small label, so you can see them in either place. Errors work the same way: the terminal prints the error with the file and line, and the browser shows it in an overlay over the page.

Leave the dev server running in its own terminal, and stop it with Ctrl+C when you're done.

## next build

`npm run build` makes a **production build**: code that's minified, split into small files per route, and checked by TypeScript, with every page that can be made ahead of time already rendered. It ends with the **route table**, one line per route with a symbol for how it's served. `○` means static: the page was rendered once, during the build. The rendering lesson reads this table in depth. A type error or a page that can't be rendered stops the build, which is what you want: it's better for the build to fail than the site.

## next start

`npm run start` serves the last build with a production server. Some things only happen here: links prefetch the next page ahead of time, pages come from the build instead of being compiled on demand, and caching behaves the way it will for your users. So before you trust a change, especially anything about speed, caching, or what loads when, build it and try it with `next start`.

examples.explanation: The first lines are the server starting: the version of Next.js, the addresses it listens on, and the two settings from `next.config.ts`. Both addresses are `127.0.0.1`, since the server listens on loopback alone. Then comes the page: `Rendering the home page` is the `console.log`, printed here because the component ran on the server. The last line is the request: a `GET` for `/`, status 200, and how long it took, split between Next.js's own work and your code. Your browser's console shows the same message too, with a small Prerender label in front, since in development Next.js copies server logs there.

steps.title: How a request is served
steps.body:
Every later lesson changes one step of what happens between a URL and a page you can click. Seeing the whole path once, in order, gives each of those lessons a place to fit.

```diagram react-to-nextjs-request
A first visit gets HTML. Later clicks get only the RSC payload, and the layout stays on screen.
```

## 1. The route is matched

You open `/products`. The server looks for the folder in `app/` that matches the path, `app/products`, and its `page.tsx`. It collects every layout on the way down, from `app/layout.tsx` inward, so it knows the whole tree to render: the root layout, then any layout in `app/products`, then the page.

## 2. Server Components render

Recall from the React course that React can render on the server, and that a **Server Component** is one that runs only there. In the App Router every component is a Server Component unless its file says otherwise, which the lesson after next explains. The server runs them, awaiting any data they need, and turns the result into two things:

- **HTML**, so the browser can show the page before any JavaScript runs. That's what makes the first view fast and what search engines read.
- The **RSC payload**, short for React Server Components payload: a compact description of the rendered tree, with markers where client components go and the props they get. React in the browser uses it to rebuild the same tree without running your Server Components again.

Both go out in one response. The payload rides along inside the HTML, in small `script` tags at the end.

## 3. The browser shows it, then hydrates

The browser shows the HTML at once. Then it downloads the JavaScript for the **client components**, the ones that use state, effects, or event handlers, and for React itself. Only client components are in it. A Server Component's code never reaches the browser. React then **hydrates**: it matches the client components to the HTML already on screen and attaches their event handlers, so the buttons start to work. Hydration is the same step you did by hand with `hydrateRoot`, done for you.

## 4. A click fetches only the payload

Now you click a link to `/about`. The `Link` component from `next/link` stops the browser's normal full-page load. Instead, the router asks the server for just the RSC payload of the new page: the same URL with an `_rsc` parameter and an `RSC: 1` header, answered as `text/x-component` rather than HTML. React compares the new tree with the one on screen and changes only what differs. The root layout and anything else both pages share stay mounted, so their state survives, and nothing is downloaded twice. This is a **soft navigation**, like the single-page app navigations from the React course, except the new page was rendered on the server.

In a production build it's often faster still: as links scroll into view, the router **prefetches** a shell of each page they point to, so a click can show something at once, often before the server has answered. The routing lesson shows how links and prefetching work, and the rendering lessons show what goes into that shell.

## Watch it in the Network panel

Run a build with `npm run build` and `npm run start`, open DevTools, choose the Network tab, and load a page. The first row is the HTML document. Click a link, and new rows appear with `_rsc=` in their names and `text/x-component` as their type. Those are the payloads. Their Response tab shows the payload itself, a few lines per component, which the lesson on Server Components reads line by line.

examples.title: A soft navigation's request
examples.prompt: From the Network panel: the request a click on a link to `/products` sent, and the response headers, trimmed to the ones that matter. The router state tree is cut short.
examples.code:
GET /products?_rsc=iOcsZRq_pjJdkPUp HTTP/1.1
Host: 127.0.0.1:3005
RSC: 1
Next-Url: /
Next-Router-State-Tree: %5B%22%22%2C%7B%22children%22%3A%5B%22products%22...

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/x-component
Cache-Control: private, no-cache, no-store, max-age=0, must-revalidate
Vary: rsc, next-router-state-tree, next-router-prefetch, next-router-segment-prefetch, Accept-Encoding
Transfer-Encoding: chunked
examples.explanation: The `RSC: 1` header asks for the payload instead of HTML. `Next-Url` says which page you're coming from, and `Next-Router-State-Tree` describes the layouts already on screen, so the server can skip what you have. The `_rsc` value is a short hash of those headers. It gives each kind of response its own URL, so a cache in between never hands a payload to a request that wanted HTML, or the other way around. The response is `text/x-component`, the RSC payload format. `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` means it arrives in pieces as the server renders, which the lesson on fetching data builds on when it streams. You don't write any of this yourself: `Link` and the router do it. The next lesson starts at step 1 of a request's path: how the folders in `app/` become routes, and how a URL is matched to one.

recap:
- Next.js adds routing from folders, rendering modes, caching, server code, Turbopack, and image, font, and metadata tools to React.
- The App Router, in app/, is built on Server Components and is what new projects use. The older Pages Router lives in pages/.
- create-next-app sets up TypeScript, ESLint, Tailwind, the App Router, Cache Components, and the @/ alias.
- app/ holds routes, public/ is served as is, and .next/ and node_modules/ are generated and never committed.
- Only variables named NEXT_PUBLIC_ reach the browser, and they're copied in at build time.
- next dev is for building, with Fast Refresh and server logs in the terminal. Test with next build and next start before trusting a change.
- A first visit gets HTML with the RSC payload inside, then hydrates. A Link click fetches only the payload, and shared layouts stay mounted.
